oil.summary: A volatile session saw WTI surge +2.77% to $104.83 while Brent slipped -1.17% to $113.54, a widening spread reflecting intraday swings driven by competing Hormuz risk and emergency supply signals. A tanker fire in the Strait of Hormuz—reportedly caused by explosive devices—pushed Brent briefly to $117 intraday before SPR-release talk and tentative Iran diplomacy dragged it back. ANZ raised its year-end Brent target by $10 to roughly $105, while traders eye a further push toward $120. Downstream products weakened, with Heating Oil off -1.05% and RBOB -0.41%, suggesting demand caution. Corporate earnings were a standout: ExxonMobil posted $15.4 bn in Q3 profit—more than double year-ago—while BP nearly quadrupled earnings. The Baker Hughes rig count was unchanged, signaling U.S. producers remain disciplined at current prices. CME options put a 77% probability on a production cut at the next OPEC meeting.
drivers: Hormuz security: tanker attack sent Brent to $117 intraday, keeping a geopolitical risk premium firmly embedded
SPR releases and tentative Iran diplomacy capped gains, contributing to Brent's end-of-day pullback despite WTI strength
Record upstream/refining profits at ExxonMobil and BP confirm sector earnings leverage; U.S. rig count flat signals producer restraint

gas.summary: European gas continued its breakout, with TTF closing at 103.19 €/MWh (+4.67% on the day, +39.56% on the month)—its highest level since the 2022 crisis—as winter approaches against a backdrop of historically low storage. Henry Hub, by contrast, slipped -1.96% to $2.894/MMBtu, though its weekly gain of nearly +10% signals tightening domestic sentiment. The Atlantic spread is stark: U.S. producers face pressure to redirect volumes to lucrative European and Asian markets, with America's LNG export infrastructure described as facing its biggest test yet. Japan is set to displace China as the world's top LNG importer in 2026, partly because high LNG prices are deterring Chinese buyers. Japan's government separately tapped $7 bn in contingency reserves to subsidize domestic fuel costs. The flat U.S. rig count raises questions about supply responsiveness as global demand accelerates.
drivers: TTF at a four-year high above 103 €/MWh on low European storage and approaching winter demand, creating extreme transatlantic price divergence
Japan poised to become world's top LNG importer in 2026 as high prices curb Chinese demand, intensifying competition for U.S. cargoes
U.S. drilling activity stagnant per Baker Hughes, limiting near-term domestic supply response despite a near-10% weekly Henry Hub rally

power.summary: News flow and price data for Power & Carbon were limited today. EU Carbon (EUA) was essentially flat at $84.88/EUA (-0.11%), consolidating within a modest +4.26% monthly gain. The dominant story in this sector is the indirect cost-push from gas: TTF's +4.67% single-day move to 103.19 €/MWh materially raises the marginal cost of gas-fired generation across Europe, which typically lifts power prices and supports carbon permit demand as coal-to-gas switching dynamics shift. However, no direct power-price data or EUA-specific headlines were provided today, so a fuller assessment of dispatch economics and carbon market flows is not possible from today's feed.
drivers: TTF at 103.19 €/MWh (+4.67% on day) raises marginal generation costs, providing indirect upward pressure on European power prices
EUA flat at $84.88 with limited carbon-specific news; month-on-month gain of +4.26% tracks the broader energy price complex higher
